MPU6050 (page 7): Document Number: PS-MPU-6000A-00 MPU-6000/MPU-6050 Product Specification Revision: 3.1 Release Date: 10/24/2011 3 Product Overview 3.1 MPU-60X0 Overview The MPU-60X0 Motion Processing Unit is the world’s first motion processing solution with integrated 9-Axis sensor fusion using its field-proven and proprietary MotionFusion™ engine for handset and tablet applications, game controllers, motion pointer remote controls, and other consumer devices. The MPU-60X0 has an embedded 3-axis MEMS gyroscope, a 3-axis MEMS accelerometer, and a Digital Motion Processor™ (DMP™) hardware accelerator engine with an auxiliary I2C port that interfaces to 3rd party digital sensors such as magnetometers. When connected to a 3-axis magnetometer, the MPU-60X0 delivers a complete 9-axis MotionFusion output to its primary I2C or SPI port (SPI is available on MPU-6000 only). The MPU-60X0 combines acceleration and rotational motion plus heading information into a single data stream for the application. This MotionProcessing™ technology

MPU6050 (page 7): or SPI port (SPI is available on MPU-6000 only). The MPU-60X0 combines acceleration and rotational motion plus heading information into a single data stream for the application. This MotionProcessing™ technology integration provides a smaller footprint and has inherent cost advantages compared to discrete gyroscope plus accelerometer solutions. The MPU-60X0 is also designed to interface with multiple non-inertial digital sensors, such as pressure sensors, on its auxiliary I2C port. The MPU-60X0 is a 2nd generation motion processor and is footprint compatible with the MPU- 30X0 family. The MPU-60X0 features three 16-bit analog-to-digital converters (ADCs) for digitizing the gyroscope outputs and three 16-bit ADCs for digitizing the accelerometer outputs. For precision tracking of both fast and slow motions, the parts feature a user-programmable gyroscope full-scale range of ±250, ±500, ±1000, and ±2000°/sec (dps) and a user-programmable accelerometer full-scale range of ±2g, ±4g,

MPU6050 (page 7): of both fast and slow motions, the parts feature a user-programmable gyroscope full-scale range of ±250, ±500, ±1000, and ±2000°/sec (dps) and a user-programmable accelerometer full-scale range of ±2g, ±4g, ±8g, and ±16g. An on-chip 1024 Byte FIFO buffer helps lower system power consumption by allowing the system processor to read the sensor data in bursts and then enter a low-power mode as the MPU collects more data. With all the necessary on-chip processing and sensor components required to support many motion-based use cases, the MPU-60X0 uniquely supports a variety of advanced motion-based applications entirely on-chip. The MPU-60X0 thus enables low-power MotionProcessing in portable applications with reduced processing requirements for the system processor. By providing an integrated MotionFusion output, the DMP in the MPU-60X0 offloads the intensive MotionProcessing computation requirements from the system processor, minimizing the need for frequent polling of the motion sensor output. Communication with all registers of the device is performed using either I2C at 400kHz or SPI at 1MHz (MPU-6000 only). For applications requiring faster communications, the sensor and interrupt registers may be read using SPI at 20MHz (MPU-6000 only). Additional features include an embedded temperature sensor and an on-chip oscillator with ±1% variation over the operating temperature range. By leveraging its patented and volume-proven Nasiri-Fabrication platform, which integrates MEMS wafers with companion CMOS electronics through wafer-level bonding, InvenSense has driven the MPU-60X0 package size down to a revolutionary footprint of 4x4x0.9mm (QFN), while providing the highest performance, lowest noise, and the lowest cost semiconductor packaging

MPU6050 (page 7): wafer-level bonding, InvenSense has driven the MPU-60X0 package size down to a revolutionary footprint of 4x4x0.9mm (QFN), while providing the highest performance, lowest noise, and the lowest cost semiconductor packaging required for handheld consumer electronic devices. The part features a robust 10,000g shock tolerance, and has programmable low-pass filters for the gyroscopes, accelerometers, and the on-chip temperature sensor. For power supply flexibility, the MPU-60X0 operates from VDD power supply voltage range of 2.375V-3.46V. Additionally, the MPU-6050 provides a VLOGIC reference pin (in addition to its analog supply pin: VDD), which sets the logic levels of its I2C interface. The VLOGIC voltage may be 1.8V±5% or VDD. The MPU-6000 and MPU-6050 are identical, except that the MPU-6050 supports the I2C serial interface only, and has a separate VLOGIC reference pin. The full-scale range of the gyro sensors may be digitally programmed to ±250, ±500, ±1000, or ±2000 degrees per second (dps). RPLiDAR A1M8 (page 3): Intro duction RPLIDAR A1 is a low cost 360 degree 2D laser scanner (LIDAR) solution developed by SLAMTEC. The system can perform 360degree scan within 6meter range. It can work excellent in all kinds of indoor environment and outdoor environment without sunlight. System connection RPLIDAR A1 contains a range scanner system and a motor system. Mechanism RPLIDAR is based on laser triangulation ranging principle and uses high-speed vision acquisition and processing hardware developed by SLAMTEC. The system measures distance data in more than 2000 times’ per second and with high resolution distance output (<1% of the distance). RPLIDAR emits modulated infrared laser signal and the laser signal is then reflected by the object to be detected. Calibration and results - Straight-line speed: - 55% power: 160 cm in 2 s, about 0.80 m/s. - A 0.2 m/s speed command gave 60 cm in 3 s, which matches the command.

Calibration and results - Turning on the spot: - 30% power: barely turns. - 35% power: about 0.4 rad/s. - 38-40% power: about 0.5 rad/s. - 65% power: about 2.4 rad/s. On-spot turns need about 32-35% power to start.

Calibration and results - First full test run (before the final fixes): - 16 of 20 goals reached in one 10-minute run. 27 goals were sent in total. 7 were sent while the LiDAR was disconnected, so they could not start and are not counted. - 4 misses: 3 goals stopped because the LiDAR dropped during the trip (the rover stopped itself, as designed), and 1 got stuck in a tight turn. Both causes were fixed after this run. - Total autonomous travel 34+ m, added over the 16 reached goals as straight-line distances from start to goal. The real driven path is longer. Longest single trip 5.4 m, and three trips were over 5 m. - Average speed on the long trips about 0.13-0.18 m/s (for example 5.4 m in about 30 s). - The goal counts come from the Nav2 log on the Pi ("Goal succeeded", "Transform data too old", "Failed to make progress"). - This was the initial result. The misses showed exactly what to fix: the LiDAR drops (motor noise) and the stalled tight turn (weak turning power).
chunks.location: First full test run (before the final fixes)

chunks.text: Calibration and results - Final run (after all the fixes): - 20 of 20 goals reached, with no LiDAR drops. - By the final run, all the fixes in our workflow were in place: noise capacitors on the motors, driver and converter; our custom-made LiDAR cable reconnected; the LiDAR guard v3; a stronger curve setting (6.0); the scan gate; and the faster Nav2 settings (0.40 m/s, rectangle footprint). - The Pi's kernel log showed only one USB reset in the final session, and that was our own test of the guard. - The rover was also demonstrated live at the Open Day: manual control, real-time mapping, and navigation on live and saved maps.
Calibration and results - LiDAR dropouts: 3 dropouts caused by motor noise in the first 10-minute test run. 0 in the final run. Measured from the LiDAR guard log and the Pi kernel log.

Calibration and results - WiFi: Before the fix: 9 of 10 pings lost, and the one that arrived took 1190 ms. After switching off WiFi power saving: 171 of 171 pings arrived while driving, 11 ms on average.
Calibration and results - Pi 5 load: While running SLAM and Nav2: 48-52 C, never throttled (throttled=0x0), load average about 1-2 out of 4 cores. LiDAR end-to-end rate about 6.85 Hz.

Calibration and results - Known limits of these results: - Each result (16 of 20 first, 20 of 20 final) comes from a single run, not from many repeated runs. - Goal accuracy uses the rover's own SLAM position. It was not checked with a tape measure. - The Gazebo simulation was used to check the software, not to measure performance numbers.

Problems and fixes - LiDAR disconnects during turns (motor noise): Symptom: during on-spot turns or sudden stops, the LiDAR USB connection dropped. In RViz the wheels turned white and the map stopped updating. Nav2 aborted goals with "Transform data too old", and the collision monitor stopped the rover. Cause: electrical noise (EMI) from the motors. The kernel log (dmesg) showed "usb ... disabled by hub (EMI?)". It happened on both the blue USB 3.0 and black USB 2.0 ports. The 4-wheel skid-steer design pulls much more current in on-spot turns than the earlier 2-wheel design with a ball caster, because the wheels slide sideways. Fixes, in the order we did them: 1. A LiDAR guard script that restarts the LiDAR automatically when scans stop. Version 3 finds the LiDAR by its stable USB ID, resets its USB straight away, and asks for a replug only if the USB does not come back. 2. Noise capacitors soldered at the sources: a 0.1 uF ceramic (code 104) across each of the 4 motors, 470 uF (25 V) + 0.1 uF across the TB6612 VM and GND pins, and 1000 uF + 0.1 uF across the converter's 5 V output to the Pi. After this, drops became much rarer. 3. Reconnected our custom-made LiDAR cable. Result: 3 LiDAR dropouts in the first 10-minute test run, 0 in the final session. Check command: sudo

Problems and fixes - LiDAR disconnects during turns (motor noise): uF across the converter's 5 V output to the Pi. After this, drops became much rarer. 3. Reconnected our custom-made LiDAR cable. Result: 3 LiDAR dropouts in the first 10-minute test run, 0 in the final session. Check command: sudo dmesg | grep -iE "EMI|disconnect"

Problems and fixes - IMU freezes after the motors stop: Symptom: the MPU6050 IMU on I2C stops answering after the motors stop, and does not recover. Test: standing still, 0% of readings failed. Driving straight at only 21% power for about 2 seconds, the IMU froze completely, and no software retry brought it back. Only cutting its power did. Tried: slower I2C (50 kHz), retries and re-wake in the IMU program, a different timeout, gentle motor ramps, powering the Pi from a wall adapter, and the noise capacitors. The capacitors helped (before them it froze every time the motors stopped), but 2-19% of readings still fail while the motors run, and it can still freeze after they stop. Why the IMU suffers more than the LiDAR: I2C is a slow, unprotected connection on two loose wires, so motor noise gets in easily, and the IMU chip locks up until its power is cut. Status: paused. Navigation does not use it (USE_IMU = False). Next ideas, in order: a 0.1 uF + 10 uF capacitor right at the IMU board with short twisted wires kept away from the motor wires; powering the IMU from a GPIO pin so the program can switch it off and on when it freezes; or reading it on an ESP32 and sending the data to the Pi over USB.

chunks.text: Problems and fixes - Map and rover missing in RViz: Symptom: RViz showed the LiDAR scans, but no map and no rover model. Map display showed a warning with width and height 0. Cause: the launch file set FASTDDS_BUILTIN_TRANSPORTS=UDPv4. This forced large messages (the map and the robot description) through the WSL network layer, where they failed. Small messages like scans still worked. Fix: removed that line from the launch file and rebuilt.
chunks.location: Map and rover missing in RViz

chunks.text: Problems and fixes - Odometry ran backwards: Symptom: when the real rover drove forward, the rover in RViz moved backwards, and SLAM drew walls twice. Cause: the LiDAR faces backwards. The laser odometry (rf2o) reads the LiDAR position only once, from the first scan. After moving everything onto the Pi, programs started faster, and the first scan sometimes arrived before the robot model was loaded. So the odometry assumed the LiDAR faced forward. Fix: a scan gate. It holds scans back from the laser odometry until the LiDAR position is known, then waits 3 more seconds. SLAM and Nav2 still get scans directly. How to check: the launch prints "Scans now go to the laser odometry." If it prints "base_footprint passed to lookupTransform ... does not exist", stop and start again.

Problems and fixes - WiFi lag and packet loss: Symptom: about 1.2 s delay and 90% packet loss between the laptop and the Pi. Navigation froze when SLAM and Nav2 ran on the laptop. Cause: WiFi power saving on the Pi. The WiFi chip sleeps between transmissions. Fix: switch off power saving at every boot (iw dev wlan0 set power_save off, run from a boot job). Also moved SLAM and Nav2 onto the Pi, so the laptop only shows RViz. Result: 171 of 171 pings arrived while driving, about 11 ms on average.

Problems and fixes - Skid-steer turns stall: Symptom: slow on-spot turns stopped halfway. Cause: a skid-steer rover needs high power to start turning, because the wheels must slide sideways. On-spot turns need about 32-35% power just to start. Fix: in the motor node, a short kick at 42% power, then a sustain power of at least 38% with a re-kick every 1.5 s. Slew ramps keep speed changes gentle.

Problems and fixes - Curves too weak while driving: Symptom: the rover did not follow the green path on curves. It drove almost straight, drifted off, stopped, spun on the spot and tried again. It looked stuck. Cause: Nav2 asked for its strongest curve, but the left and right sides differed by only 8% power (curve gain 2.0). A 4-wheel skid-steer rover needs a much bigger difference to curve. Fix: curve gain raised to 6.0. At Nav2's strongest curve the sides now differ by about 25%, and the rover follows the path.

Problems and fixes - Too slow, and obstacle boundaries too thick: Symptom: the rover never went above 0.20 m/s, and the safety zones around walls were thick and messy, leaving little room in gaps. Fix: Nav2 top speed 0.40 m/s for straight driving (turns stay slow). The rover's real shape, a 30 x 26 cm rectangle, instead of a 40 cm circle. Obstacles marked only up to 2.5 m away, because far points are the noisiest. Safety zone 0.30 m. In RViz, the global costmap display is switched off for a cleaner view.
chunks.location: Too slow, and obstacle boundaries too thick

chunks.text: Problems and fixes - Wheels shown white in RViz: Symptom: the wheels in RViz were white with a RobotModel error. Cause: the program that publishes wheel positions sometimes missed the model at start. The real rover has no wheel sensors anyway. Fix: the wheels are fixed parts of the model on the real rover. They still turn in the simulation.

Problems and fixes - Map drawn twice (star pattern): Symptom: walls appear twice in a star-like pattern. Cause: a LiDAR drop in the middle of a turn, or lifting the rover. Without encoders or an IMU, SLAM depends only on matching scans, and a large angle error is more than it can correct. Fix: restart SLAM for a fresh map, keep the rover still at start, and drive gently.
Problems and fixes - Nav2 hangs at start: Symptom: "failed to send response to /<node>/change_state (timeout)", or goals are ignored. Fix: stop the navigation launch with Ctrl+C and start it again.

Problems and fixes - RViz window does not appear (COPY MODE): Symptom: on the WSL laptop, RViz or Gazebo shows only a taskbar icon or "COPY MODE", or freezes. Fix: close it, run wsl --shutdown in PowerShell, wait 30 seconds, open Ubuntu again and test with xeyes.
chunks.location: RViz window does not appear (COPY MODE)

chunks.text: Problems and fixes - Laptop cannot see the Pi topics: Symptom: the laptop cannot see /scan from the Pi. Cause: WSL lost network visibility after wsl --shutdown, or the Windows network profile for the hotspot was set to Public, which can block ROS discovery. Fix: restart WSL, check ping, and set the network profile to Private.
chunks.location: Laptop cannot see the Pi topics

chunks.text: Problems and fixes - Hardware PWM failed with "Invalid argument": Symptom: writing the PWM period on the Pi 5 failed. Cause: wrong PWM channel numbers, and the pwm-2chan overlay was missing its clock setting. Fix: use the right channels for the soldered pins (GPIO18 and GPIO19), and keep dtoverlay=pwm-2chan,clock=50000000 in config.txt.

Problems and fixes - Left motor ran backwards: Cause: the left motor is mounted as a mirror image of the right. Fix: LEFT_INVERTED = True in the motor code, which swaps the direction pins in software.

Problems and fixes - Mechanical issues still open: - The front-left wheel was stiff and was refitted once. - The left side is weaker than the right. - In turns, the front wheels barely roll, and the rover pivots near the front axle.

Rover overview - What the rover does: The rover builds a map of an unknown indoor space while it drives (SLAM), and then drives itself to any goal clicked on that map (Nav2). It uses one 2D LiDAR as its main sensor. There are no wheel encoders. Motion is tracked by comparing LiDAR scans (laser odometry with rf2o). Everything (LiDAR driver, motor control, SLAM and Nav2) runs on the Raspberry Pi 5. The laptop only shows the map in RViz.

Rover overview - What we demonstrated: - Manual driving with the keyboard. - Real-time mapping with SLAM Toolbox while driving. - Autonomous navigation to goals on the live map, and on a saved map. - All of these both in the Gazebo simulation and on the real rover.

Rover overview - Where it could be used: Mapping a building after a disaster (fire, gas leak, partial collapse) before people go in, and showing rescuers a safe route. This links to SDG 11 (safer cities and communities). A second use is mapping warehouse or factory floors and reaching inspection points (SDG 9). For real rubble it would need bigger wheels, a 3D sensor and an IMU. The mapping and navigation software would stay the same.

Rover overview - Team and guide: Team 6: Abdul Rahman Khan, M. Yashwanth and Pranav Pujari, Department of AI and ML, Global Academy of Technology, Bengaluru. Guide: Prof. Vijaya Dalawai, Assistant Professor, Dept of AIML. Project title: Autonomous Mobile Rover with Real-Time Mapping and Navigation.

Rover overview - Main parts: - Computer: Raspberry Pi 5, 4 GB, running Ubuntu Server 24.04 and ROS 2 Jazzy. - LiDAR: Slamtec RPLiDAR A1M8, 360 degree 2D laser scanner, connected over USB with our own custom-made cable to its adapter board, about 6.85 scans per second on our rover. - Motor driver: TB6612FNG dual H-bridge. One board drives all 4 motors and stays cool. - Motors: 4 x 12 V BO gear motors, 200 RPM. - Power: 3S LiPo battery, 2200 mAh (11.1 V nominal, 12.6 V full), and an XY-3606 5 V converter for the Pi. - IMU: MPU6050 on I2C. Wired, but switched off for now (see the problems notes). - Noise capacitors: 0.1 uF ceramic (104) on each motor, 470 uF + 0.1 uF on the driver's motor supply, 1000 uF + 0.1 uF on the converter's 5 V output.

Rover overview - Drive type: The rover is 4-wheel drive with skid steering. There are no steering wheels. It turns like a tank: the left and right sides run at different speeds. The left pair of motors is on driver channel A and the right pair on channel B. Front and rear motors on each side are wired together.

Rover overview - Measurements: - Length 28 cm, width 24.5 cm. Nav2 uses a 30 x 26 cm rectangle as the rover's shape. - Wheelbase (front axle to rear axle): 18 cm. - Track (left tyre centre to right tyre centre): 22 cm. - Wheel size: 11 cm. - LiDAR: 8.5 cm in front of the rover centre, laser height 21.5 cm above the floor. - The LiDAR is mounted facing backwards (rotated 180 degrees). The robot model file tells the software this.

Rover overview - Software pipeline: 1. LiDAR driver publishes scans on the /scan topic. 2. A scan gate holds scans until the robot model is loaded, then passes them to the laser odometry. 3. Laser odometry (rf2o) compares each scan with the previous one to estimate how far the rover moved and turned. 4. SLAM Toolbox builds the map (5 cm squares, updated every 2 seconds) and corrects the rover position. 5. Nav2 plans a path on the map and follows it with the Regulated Pure Pursuit controller. 6. The motor node turns Nav2 speed commands into PWM power for the left and right sides. 7. A LiDAR guard script (version 3) watches the scans. If they stop, it resets the LiDAR's USB and restarts the LiDAR program.

Rover overview - Nav2 settings: - Top speed 0.40 m/s for straight driving. Nav2 slows down on curves and near obstacles. - Turning speed about 0.6 rad/s. - Rover shape: a 30 x 26 cm rectangle (earlier a 40 cm circle). - Obstacles are marked only up to 2.5 m away, because far LiDAR points are the noisiest. - Safety zone (inflation) around obstacles: 0.30 m. - A goal counts as reached when the heading is within about 20 degrees (0.35 rad).

Rover overview - Motor node settings: - Minimum duty 10%, maximum duty 80%. - Turning on the spot: a short kick at 42% power, then at least 38% sustain power (plus 0.08 per 1 rad/s asked), with a re-kick every 1.5 s so slow turns do not stall. - Turning while driving: curve gain 6.0 (raised from 2.0, which was too weak for skid steer). - Gentle slew ramps for speed changes. - Safety timeout 0.5 s: motors stop if no command arrives.

Rover overview - Limits: - Indoor only. Strong sunlight confuses the A1M8, and laser odometry needs walls to compare against. - The LiDAR sees one flat slice at 21.5 cm height. Obstacles lower than about 25 cm may not be seen. - No wheel encoders and no IMU at present, so fast turns can smear the map. - Do not lift the rover while SLAM is running. It spoils the map.

Simulation work - Isaac Sim warehouse rover: We started in NVIDIA Isaac Sim 5.1, installed with pip in a Python virtual environment on the lab PC (RTX A2000 12 GB). The script warehouse_rover.py places a Nova Carter rover in the Simple Warehouse scene. It drives to 4 coloured waste objects using an Artificial Potential Field (APF) planner written in pure Python, with no ROS 2. The goal pulls the rover towards it, and obstacles push it away. At each object it plays a 3-second pickup animation (the object shrinks until it disappears). A second script, rover_simulation.py, builds procedural grassy uneven terrain.

Simulation work - Two-layer simulation idea: The world can be detailed and realistic (RTX rendering, rich terrain). The robot model must behave like the real hardware, including servo backlash, encoder drift and sensor noise. This keeps simulation results honest.

Simulation work - Gazebo digital twin of the real rover: For the real rover, we built a Gazebo Harmonic simulation with ROS 2 Jazzy, running in WSL2 (Ubuntu 24.04) on a laptop. It uses the same robot model file as the real rover (body, 4 wheels and LiDAR position from real measurements). The simulated hardware has skid-steer drive for 4 wheels and a LiDAR at about 7 scans per second, like the A1M8. One launch file (sim_slam_nav.launch.py) starts Gazebo, the rover, the ROS-Gazebo bridge, the scan gate, laser odometry, SLAM Toolbox, Nav2 and RViz in the right order. There are two worlds: a corridor with obstacles and an empty world. An option switches between laser odometry and Gazebo's wheel odometry, to compare the two. The simulation uses the same Nav2 settings file as the real rover.

chunks.text: Simulation work - How the simulation was used: The same ROS 2 software mapped the Gazebo world and reached goals there. We used the simulation to check the software before moving it to the real rover, not to measure performance numbers. In simulation, all programs run on the laptop, so it does not prove the Pi can handle the load. That was checked separately on the real rover.
Simulation work - Separate ROS channel: The simulation runs on ROS_DOMAIN_ID 7. Even if the real rover is switched on, the simulation can never send commands to it, and the maps never mix.

Simulation work - What the simulation did not show: Five real problems never appeared in simulation: WiFi power-save lag, navigation freezing over WiFi, backwards odometry from the start-up timing on the Pi, motor noise dropping the LiDAR USB, and stalled skid-steer turns. This is the main sim-to-real lesson of the project.

chunks.text: Our workflow, 19. (Making it work on the real rover) Noise capacitors fitted. Soldered capacitors at the noise sources: a 0.1 uF ceramic (104) across each of the 4 motors, 470 uF + 0.1 uF across the TB6612 motor supply (VM and GND), and 1000 uF + 0.1 uF across the converter's 5 V output to the Pi. After this, the LiDAR dropped much less often during turns. Status: Done. Area: Electronics.
